title: Recall bank, Q404–457
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall bank, questions 404–457. Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A preterm baby has stage 2 retinopathy of prematurity. What should the family be told?
questions.a: He will only need glasses in the future
questions.e: He needs regular follow-up eye examinations and may need treatment
questions.exp: Stage 2 ROP (a ridge) often regresses, but it can progress, so screening continues every 1–2 weeks until the retina is fully vascularised. Treatment (laser or anti-VEGF injection) is needed for type 1 ROP, such as zone I disease with plus disease or stage 3, or zone II stage 2–3 with plus disease. Children who had ROP also have more myopia and squint later.

questions.question: A neonate has an exchange transfusion with citrated blood. Which electrolyte problem is common during the procedure?
questions.exp: Citrate binds calcium, so hypocalcaemia (jitteriness, arrhythmia) is common; monitor ionised calcium. Other complications: hypoglycaemia then rebound, hyperkalaemia, thrombocytopenia, infection, air embolism, portal vein thrombosis, NEC and volume problems.

questions.question: At what age should screening with transcranial Doppler ultrasound start in children with sickle cell anaemia?
questions.exp: Transcranial Doppler screening is done every year from 2 to 16 years of age in HbSS and HbS-beta0 thalassaemia. A high middle cerebral artery velocity (above 200 cm/s) shows a high stroke risk, and regular blood transfusion then cuts the stroke risk by about 90%.

questions.question: A boy has juvenile dermatomyositis. Which long-term complication is typical?
questions.exp: Juvenile dermatomyositis: proximal weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, raised CK. Calcinosis (calcium deposits in skin and muscle) affects up to 30–40%, more with delayed or inadequate treatment; lipodystrophy and vasculopathy are other complications. Uveitis is typical of oligoarticular JIA, and amyloidosis of untreated FMF.

questions.question: A teenage girl with obsessive–compulsive disorder washes her hands many times a day. Which drug is used?
questions.exp: OCD treatment: cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention, adding an SSRI (fluoxetine, sertraline) if needed. Antipsychotics are used only as augmentation in resistant cases.

questions.question: A child with cerebral palsy comes in with a dislodged gastrostomy tube. There is no tube with him, the stoma looks moist and there is no infection. What should be done?
questions.a: Leave the stoma to close and plan a new gastrostomy
questions.b: Cover with a dry dressing only
questions.c: Insert a urinary (Foley) catheter into the stoma to keep it open
questions.d: Discharge him and ask him to come back another day
questions.exp: The tract can close within hours. Put a Foley catheter or a spare gastrostomy tube into the stoma to keep the tract open until a proper tube can be replaced and its position confirmed.

questions.question: A 9-month-old is pale but otherwise well. Hb is 9 g/dL, and the blood film shows small, pale red cells. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Iron deficiency is the most common cause of anaemia at this age (prolonged milk feeding, especially cow's milk, and poor weaning). The film shows microcytic hypochromic cells with pencil cells. Give oral iron (3–6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron) for 3 months after Hb normalises, and limit milk to about 500 mL a day.

questions.question: A neonate has firm, red-purple nodules and plaques on the back after a difficult delivery with cooling. Which complication should be checked for?
questions.exp: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn appears in the first weeks on the back, shoulders and buttocks, after asphyxia, cooling or trauma. It resolves by itself, but hypercalcaemia can develop up to 6 months later (vomiting, poor feeding, nephrocalcinosis), so check calcium regularly.

questions.question: A child is found unconscious and admitted to intensive care. The ECG monitor shows a QRS duration of 150 ms. A tricyclic antidepressant overdose is suspected. Which drug should be given?
questions.exp: Tricyclics block cardiac sodium channels, widening the QRS (above 100 ms predicts seizures, above 160 ms ventricular arrhythmias). IV sodium bicarbonate (1–2 mmol/kg) raises pH and sodium and narrows the QRS. Avoid class IA/IC antiarrhythmics, and flumazenil (seizures). Dilated pupils with anticholinergic features are typical.

questions.question: A child has had fever and night sweats for 6–8 weeks. There are three cervical lymph nodes, each 2–3 cm, firm, non-tender and fixed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Red flags in lymphadenopathy: nodes over 2 cm, hard, fixed or matted, supraclavicular, growing over 2–4 weeks, or with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) or hepatosplenomegaly. Do a chest X-ray, blood count and LDH, then an excision biopsy. TB nodes are often matted, may become fluctuant and drain, with a positive TB test.

questions.question: A child has body aches and headache. Blood tests show neutropenia or lymphopenia, and the blood culture grows Gram-negative coccobacilli. Which history supports the diagnosis?
questions.e: Contact with someone with a chronic cough
questions.exp: Brucellosis comes from unpasteurised dairy products or contact with infected animals. It causes fever, sweats, arthralgia, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias. Treat with combination antibiotics for at least 6 weeks.

questions.question: A teenager has dizziness, chest pain, breathlessness and palpitations. The ECG shows a coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with a right bundle branch block pattern. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Brugada syndrome (SCN5A sodium channel, autosomal dominant) shows coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with pseudo-RBBB, which can be brought out by fever. It causes syncope and sudden death from ventricular fibrillation. Treat fever promptly, avoid sodium-channel blocking drugs, and an ICD is needed after cardiac arrest or arrhythmic syncope.

questions.question: A tall boy has delayed puberty and cannot smell (anosmia). Which result supports the diagnosis of Kallmann syndrome?
questions.a: Low LH and FSH with low testosterone
questions.e: High LH and FSH with low testosterone
questions.exp: Kallmann syndrome is hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (GnRH neurons fail to migrate) with anosmia: low LH, FSH and sex steroids, and absent or small olfactory bulbs on MRI. Boys are often eunuchoid (tall, long limbs) with small testes or cryptorchidism. High LH and FSH would mean primary gonadal failure (Klinefelter, 47,XXY).

questions.question: A child with asplenia needs pneumococcal protection. Which schedule is right?
questions.a: No pneumococcal vaccine is needed if he takes penicillin
questions.b: Two doses of polysaccharide vaccine only
questions.c: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine first, then the polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) at least 8 weeks later
questions.d: Polysaccharide vaccine first, then the conjugate vaccine 8 weeks later
questions.e: Two doses of conjugate vaccine only
questions.exp: Give the conjugate vaccine first (it primes a T-cell-dependent memory response), then PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later (from age 2), with a second PPSV23 dose 5 years later. Giving the polysaccharide vaccine first can blunt the response to later doses. Penicillin prophylaxis is added, not a substitute.

questions.question: A 12-year-old obese girl has no periods yet and has acne. There is no acanthosis nigricans, and she has milk discharge from the breasts. Which test supports the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Galactorrhoea with amenorrhoea suggests hyperprolactinaemia (prolactinoma, drugs such as antipsychotics, hypothyroidism). Check prolactin, TFTs and a pregnancy test; if prolactin is high without a drug cause, do an MRI of the pituitary. Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are first-line for prolactinoma.

questions.question: A girl has a breast bud with the areola beginning to enlarge, and a few sparse hairs on the labia and lower pubis. What is her Tanner stage?
questions.exp: Breast 2 = breast bud with enlargement of the areola; pubic hair 2 = sparse, long, slightly pigmented hair mainly on the labia. Breast 3 = further growth of breast and areola as one mound; breast 4 = areola and nipple form a secondary mound; breast 5 = adult contour.

questions.question: A 13-year-old girl has not started her periods. The nipple and areola form a secondary mound projecting above the breast. What Tanner stage is this?
questions.exp: Breast stage 4: the areola and nipple form a secondary mound above the level of the breast. Menarche usually happens at breast stage 4, about 2–2.5 years after thelarche, so she is still within normal limits. Primary amenorrhoea is investigated if there are no periods by 15 years with normal secondary sex characteristics, or by 13 with none.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl has microscopic haematuria (blood ++) on a urine dipstick, with no protein, nitrite or leucocytes. She is well with normal blood pressure. What should be done?
questions.b: Repeat the urine test and arrange a renal and bladder ultrasound
questions.exp: Isolated microscopic haematuria in a well child is often transient or benign (thin basement membrane disease, hypercalciuria). Confirm on repeat samples with microscopy, check BP, urine calcium:creatinine, renal function and family history, and do an ultrasound. Cystoscopy is almost never needed in children. Biopsy is for proteinuria, hypertension, or renal impairment.

questions.question: After a car accident a child has unequal pupils, blood pressure 170/100, heart rate 70 and respiratory rate 15. What should be done first?
questions.e: Give hypertonic (3%) saline (or mannitol) and secure the airway
questions.exp: Hypertension with a relatively slow heart rate and abnormal breathing (Cushing triad) plus unequal pupils means raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation. Protect the airway (intubate), give 3% saline 3–5 mL/kg or mannitol, raise the head of the bed, avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia, then urgent CT and neurosurgery. Do not treat the BP, which is maintaining brain perfusion.

questions.question: An 8-month-old has a subconjunctival haemorrhage and petechiae near the ear. There is no cough or vomiting. What should be done?
questions.a: Check a full blood count only and discharge if normal
questions.b: Give antibiotics for possible meningococcal infection
questions.c: Arrange an eye clinic review in 2 weeks
questions.e: Refer to the child protection team and do a full safeguarding assessment, including blood tests
questions.exp: Petechiae on the face, neck or ears and subconjunctival haemorrhage in an infant without coughing, vomiting or a bleeding disorder suggest strangulation, slapping or squeezing. Any bruise or petechiae in a non-mobile baby needs a safeguarding referral, a full examination, FBC and clotting, and often skeletal survey and CT head.

questions.question: A child in intensive care died after being given 10 times the recommended dose of morphine. What should be done?
questions.a: Blame the nurse who gave the drug
questions.b: Hide the error to protect the team
questions.c: Openly disclose the error to the family, apologise and report it
questions.d: Wait for the post-mortem before speaking to the family
questions.e: Tell the family only if they ask
questions.exp: The duty of candour requires honest, prompt disclosure of an error that caused harm, with an apology, an explanation of what happened and what will be done. The incident must be reported (and to the coroner when a death may be caused by an error), and investigated to improve systems, not to blame individuals.

questions.question: A 4-year-old has had a wet cough for 8 weeks. Salbutamol and a short course of antibiotics did not help. He is otherwise well. What should be done?
questions.c: A 2-week course of amoxicillin–clavulanate for protracted bacterial bronchitis
questions.exp: A chronic wet cough (over 4 weeks) in a well child with no red flags is most often protracted bacterial bronchitis (H. influenzae, Moraxella, pneumococcus): treat with 2 weeks (up to 4) of amoxicillin–clavulanate. If it fails, investigate further (chest X-ray, sweat test, immunology, bronchoscopy). A clear history of choking or focal signs means bronchoscopy for a foreign body first.

questions.question: A fully vaccinated 5-year-old (DTaP booster at 4 years) steps on a nail. The wound is dirty and bleeding. What is needed?
questions.c: Clean the wound well; no tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin is needed
questions.d: Oral antibiotics for all puncture wounds
questions.exp: For a tetanus-prone wound: if the child is fully immunised and the last dose was less than 5 years ago, no vaccine is needed (some guidelines say less than 10 years). Give a booster if more than 5 years, and add tetanus immunoglobulin only if the immunisation is incomplete or unknown and the wound is high risk. Clean and debride the wound; antibiotics if infected. Nail injuries through a shoe can cause Pseudomonas osteomyelitis.

questions.question: A 3-year-old with sickle cell disease has never been vaccinated. Which pneumococcal vaccine should be given first?
questions.exp: Functional asplenia in sickle cell disease brings a high risk of pneumococcal sepsis. Catch up with the conjugate vaccine first, then PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later (age 2 or older), plus Hib, meningococcal and yearly influenza vaccines and daily penicillin prophylaxis until at least 5 years.

questions.question: In refeeding syndrome, what is the main cause of death?
questions.exp: Hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, with fluid retention in a wasted heart, cause arrhythmias and congestive cardiac failure, the main causes of death. Monitor ECG and electrolytes daily during early refeeding.

questions.question: An adolescent athlete has pain and swelling below the left knee during exercise, with a tender tibial tuberosity and no joint effusion. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Osgood–Schlatter disease: traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in growing, active adolescents, with a tender bump and pain on activity, without effusion. Meniscal tears cause locking and an effusion; shin splints cause diffuse pain along the medial tibia.

questions.question: A malnourished child has severe wasting and bilateral pitting oedema of the legs. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bilateral pitting oedema in a malnourished child defines oedematous severe acute malnutrition (kwashiorkor), whatever the weight. Other features: skin changes (flaky paint dermatosis), sparse depigmented hair, a fatty liver and apathy. Marasmus is severe wasting without oedema. Manage with the WHO 10 steps (F-75 then F-100 or RUTF, careful fluids, antibiotics).

questions.question: A child has X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets. PTH is normal, alkaline phosphatase is high and there is a family history. Which statement is correct?
questions.b: Treatment is high-dose vitamin D alone
questions.c: Urinary phosphate loss is high (low TmP/GFR)
questions.e: A son of an affected father has a 25% chance of being affected
questions.exp: X-linked hypophosphataemia (PHEX, high FGF23): low serum phosphate from renal phosphate wasting (low TmP/GFR), high ALP, normal calcium and PTH, and an inappropriately low-normal 1,25-vitamin D. Affected fathers pass it to all daughters and no sons; affected mothers to 50% of children. Treatment: burosumab (anti-FGF23), or oral phosphate with calcitriol.

questions.question: A 4-year-old says only 3–4 words but understands and follows instructions, plays well and has normal motor development. What is the next step?
questions.exp: A 4-year-old should speak in sentences. Isolated expressive language delay with good understanding and play needs a formal hearing test first (hearing loss is common and treatable), then speech and language therapy referral. Social interaction and play are normal here, so autism is less likely.

questions.question: A neonate is diagnosed with necrotising enterocolitis. What should be done first?
questions.c: Stop feeds and pass a nasogastric tube on free drainage, with IV fluids and antibiotics
questions.d: Continue feeds with a lactose-free formula
questions.exp: NEC treatment: nil by mouth with gastric decompression, IV fluids and parenteral nutrition, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, serial X-rays and bloods, and surgical review. Surgery is for perforation or clinical deterioration.

questions.question: Which statement about necrotising enterocolitis is correct?
questions.b: It is a multifactorial inflammatory process of immature bowel
questions.c: It occurs mostly in term breastfed babies
questions.d: It is caused only by septicaemia
questions.exp: NEC results from immaturity of the gut, abnormal bacterial colonisation, formula feeding and impaired blood flow, causing inflammation and necrosis. Risk falls with breast milk (especially mother's own), antenatal steroids and, in some units, probiotics.

questions.question: A child has hereditary spherocytosis. What is the usual mode of inheritance?
questions.exp: Hereditary spherocytosis (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3 defects) is autosomal dominant in about 75%; the rest are recessive or new mutations. Features: haemolysis, jaundice, splenomegaly, gallstones, aplastic crises with parvovirus. Test with EMA binding. Folic acid; splenectomy for severe disease after age 6 with vaccinations.

questions.question: A well neonate has a platelet count of 15 x 10^9/L, a normal PT and a mother with a normal platelet count (suspected neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia). What is the treatment?
questions.b: Platelet transfusion (HPA-matched if available, otherwise random donor)
questions.exp: In NAIT, give platelets when the count is under 30 (or under 50 with bleeding) to prevent intracranial haemorrhage: HPA-1a/5b negative platelets if available, otherwise random donor platelets. IVIG can be added. Do a cranial ultrasound. Later pregnancies need specialist care (maternal IVIG).

questions.question: A neonate is pale but has no bleeding. Mother and baby are both O positive. What test should be done?
questions.c: Kleihauer test on the mother's blood
questions.exp: Pallor at birth with the same blood group in mother and baby (no ABO or Rh haemolysis) and no visible bleeding suggests fetomaternal haemorrhage. The Kleihauer–Betke test counts fetal red cells in the mother's blood. The Apt test tells whether blood vomited or passed by a baby is fetal or swallowed maternal blood.

questions.question: A newborn has blisters and areas of skin loss at sites of friction, with nail changes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Epidermolysis bullosa: inherited fragility of the skin, with blisters and erosions from minor friction from birth, nail dystrophy, oral blisters and, in severe forms, scarring and fusion of fingers. Handle gently, use non-adhesive dressings, pierce blisters, prevent infection. Aplasia cutis is a localised scalp defect present at birth.

questions.question: A 6-month-old girl has agenesis of the corpus callosum with motor and developmental delay and infantile spasms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Aicardi syndrome: girls, infantile spasms, agenesis of the corpus callosum, chorioretinal lacunae and severe delay. Apert is craniosynostosis with syndactyly; Sotos is overgrowth with a large head.

questions.question: On a mechanical ventilator, which setting most directly improves the PaO2?
questions.exp: Oxygenation depends on FiO2 and mean airway pressure, which is raised mainly by PEEP (and peak pressure and inspiratory time). CO2 removal depends on minute ventilation (rate x tidal volume).

questions.question: A mother with sickle cell anaemia at 39 weeks had morphine for 2 weeks before delivery. The baby was given naloxone and had a seizure 10 minutes after birth. What is the cause?
questions.a: Naloxone given to the baby, which triggered acute opioid withdrawal
questions.exp: Naloxone in a baby exposed to opioids for a long time precipitates sudden withdrawal with seizures within minutes. It is contraindicated in babies of opioid-dependent mothers; support breathing with ventilation instead.

questions.question: A neonate has metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap and a high ammonia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.b: An organic acidaemia (such as propionic or methylmalonic acidaemia)
questions.exp: Organic acidaemias cause a severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketosis, hyperammonaemia (secondary inhibition of the urea cycle), neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Urea cycle defects give hyperammonaemia WITHOUT acidosis. Send urine organic acids and plasma acylcarnitines.

questions.question: A child dies in the emergency department despite resuscitation. How should his family be told?
questions.a: Tell them in the corridor as soon as they arrive
questions.c: Ask them to calm down and wait without information
questions.d: A senior doctor meets the parents in a private room, sits down and explains that there is bad news, then tells them clearly
questions.e: Let the nursing staff tell them
questions.exp: Break bad news in a private room, sitting down, with a nurse present; give a warning shot, use the word "died", allow silence and questions, and offer support and the chance to see the child.

questions.question: An adolescent has sudden sharp chest pain and breathlessness after an accident. A haemothorax is found. What should be done first?
questions.a: Insert a large-bore chest drain and resuscitate with IV fluids and blood
questions.c: Needle decompression in the second intercostal space only
questions.exp: A haemothorax needs a chest drain (5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line) with resuscitation, including blood. Massive haemothorax or ongoing bleeding needs thoracotomy. Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance, shifted trachea, shock).

questions.question: A newborn has congenital syphilis. What is the treatment?
questions.a: A single dose of benzathine penicillin for all cases
questions.exp: Proven or probable congenital syphilis is treated with aqueous benzylpenicillin IV for 10 days (10–14 in many guidelines). Follow non-treponemal titres until negative.

questions.question: An infant has heart failure with cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly, and a bruit is heard over the skull. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation is a large arteriovenous shunt in the brain: high-output heart failure in the newborn, a cranial bruit, hydrocephalus and seizures later. Diagnose with cranial ultrasound/MRI; treat by endovascular embolisation.

questions.question: A ventilated preterm baby develops periventricular haemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia. Which type of cerebral palsy is most likely?
questions.exp: Periventricular white matter damage in preterm babies affects the leg fibres of the corticospinal tracts that run closest to the ventricles, causing spastic diplegia (legs more than arms). Dyskinetic CP follows basal ganglia injury (kernicterus, term asphyxia).

questions.question: A mother at 22 weeks learns her baby has a lethal rickets-like skeletal dysplasia. When should she be referred to paediatric palliative care?
questions.exp: Perinatal palliative care starts at diagnosis, so the family can plan the birth and comfort care.
